name: 20-20-20 rule / screen breaks

lead: The 20-20-20 rule asks screen users to look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. People follow it to ease dry, strained eyes and the red, tired look that comes with long screen days.

Looking into the distance relaxes close-focus effort, and breaks may encourage blinking, which reviews cite as relevant to dry, strained eyes. Reviews list breaks among digital eye strain management options, and a 2023 study tested the rule directly for strain and dry eye. Appearance effects have not been studied.

paras: Most people set a repeating timer or use a reminder app while working at a screen, glancing out a window or down a hallway during each break. It costs nothing and is used all day.
No harms are documented. Persistent eye symptoms are a matter for an eye-care professional.

web.title: Deconstructing the 20-20-20 rule for digital eye strain

angle.text: Regular distance breaks relax close-focus effort and encourage blinking, so screen days leave less dryness and strain and the eyes look less red and tired. The rule has been studied for strain comfort, not eye whiteness.

lead: The 20-20-20 rule is a screen-break habit: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. People adopt it to keep their eyes comfortable during long screen sessions, and in looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a free way to keep the eyes looking fresh, with less redness, strain and squinting around the eye area.[1][2]

The rule is aimed at digital eye strain, also called computer vision syndrome, a group of symptoms that includes dry, itchy or tired eyes, blurred vision and headache. The chain people describe runs from regular breaks, to less strain and dryness, to eyes that feel and look more rested. That appearance link is the community's framing; the published research measures symptoms, not how the eyes look.[3][2]

A 2023 study fitted 29 symptomatic computer users with break-reminder software based on the rule and reported improvements in digital eye strain and dry eye symptoms while the reminders were in use.[4] Reviews list breaks as one measure among several, alongside correcting refractive error, treating dry eye, blinking and ergonomics.[3][5]
infobox: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds
Credited to optometrist Jeffrey Anshel, who says he devised it around 1991 [7]
AAO advises looking up at a distant object and blinking consciously [6]
During desktop, laptop and phone work, often with a reminder app [8]

paras: The rule has three numbers: a 20-minute work interval, a 20-foot viewing distance and a 20-second pause. Looking at a distant object lets the focusing muscles used for close work relax, and the pause gives a chance to blink more fully.[2][5]

Wikipedia describes it as commonly cited advice attributed to optometrists, while noting that the article gives no specific professional guideline for it.[1] The American Academy of Ophthalmology's public advice on computer use recommends looking up from the screen from time to time at a distant object, without specifying the 20-20-20 timings.[6] Other suggestions in the same sources include deliberate blinking, artificial tears for dry eye, reducing glare, adjusting brightness and sitting roughly an arm's length from the screen.[1][5][6]

The rule is credited to the optometrist Jeffrey Anshel. In an account published in Optometry Times in 2018, Anshel said he came up with it around 1991 while lecturing corporate audiences on computer-related vision stress, and linked it to his book Visual Ergonomics in the Workplace, first published in 1998. He said he needed a way to get workers to take breaks, that it grew out of earlier 'blink, breathe, break' advice, and that the catchphrase took hold through TV and radio interviews [7].

Anshel has said that the rule does not stop or reverse myopia, and the same article's author, optometrist Brian Chou, wrote in 2018 that no peer-reviewed studies had at that time evaluated the technique; the 2023 reminder-software study came afterwards [7][4]. The Wikipedia article on computer vision syndrome calls it a common catchphrase and lists regular breaks among management options [1].

Practitioners apply the rule during desktop, laptop and phone work: a glance out of a window, across a room or down a corridor, often combined with deliberate blinking and a stretch. Reminder tools range from phone timers to software that watches for breaks, gaze and blinking, as in the 2023 study, and break-tracking apps that sync across devices have been shown on Hacker News [4][8].

In looksmaxxing and appearance discussion, the habit sits in the eye-area toolkit alongside sleep, hydration and lubricating drops: the goal described is eyes that look less red, squinted and tired by the end of the day. Practitioners report the effect as comfort first and appearance second, and the published research measures comfort-related symptoms [2][4].

Digital eye strain covers visual and ocular symptoms that arise from prolonged device use: dryness, itching, foreign-body sensation, watering, blurred vision and headache, sometimes with neck and back discomfort.[2] A 2018 review stated that prevalence may be 50% or more among computer users and divided symptoms into those linked to focusing or binocular-vision stress and external symptoms linked to dry eye.[3] A 2022 comprehensive review reported pre-pandemic prevalence ranging from 5 to 65%.[2]

A 2019 review reported that as many as 90% of device users experience some symptoms,[5] and a TFOS Lifestyle report noted figures of up to 97% in the literature, attributing the spread to the lack of an agreed definition and to limits in the questionnaires used.[9] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11,254 affected individuals estimated global prevalence at 63%.[10] A 2026 narrative review emphasises that digital eye strain (reported in 50 to 90% of regular users) and dry eye disease (5 to 50%) are related but distinct constructs.[11]

Screen use is associated with lower blink rates and more incomplete blinks, which can destabilise the tear film and contribute to dry eye.[12] The AAO says people blink about 15 times a minute normally and about 5 to 7 times a minute at screens.[6] The 2026 narrative review adds that reduced blinking appears to be driven largely by the cognitive demands of the task rather than by the screen itself, whereas incomplete blinking was higher with digital devices.[11]

Surveys during COVID-19 lockdowns reported high rates of symptoms among children and students attending online classes, and reviews noted new-onset vergence problems and myopia progression among children.[2][13][14]

Reviews of management place regular breaks among several approaches: correcting refractive error or presbyopia, treating dry eye, ergonomics, and addressing vergence or accommodation problems.[3][5] A review of preventive measures for screen-related dry eye found that frequent breaks were associated with fewer symptoms, while ergonomic training, blink animations and omega-3 supplementation improved signs and symptoms; its authors noted that no study they identified had assessed the 20-20-20 rule itself.[12]

The 2026 narrative review describes behavioural interventions including the 20-20-20 rule, along with oral omega-3, as having low-certainty evidence.[11] Research on appearance outcomes, such as eye redness or perceived tiredness in photographs, has not been published.

Public guidance varies in wording. The American Academy of Ophthalmology advises looking up from the screen at a distant object from time to time without specifying timings, and says screens do not permanently damage the eyes, while noting that long sessions can cause discomfort [6].

The main direct test is a 2023 study in Contact Lens & Anterior Eye. Webcam-based software on the laptops of 29 symptomatic computer users monitored breaks, gaze and blinking and sent personalised reminders based on the rule. Digital eye strain, binocular vision and dry eye were assessed before, after two weeks of reminders, and one week after they stopped.[4]

Participants worked for shorter stretches and took more, shorter breaks. Digital eye strain and dry eye symptoms improved, but the improvement was not sustained one week after reminders ended. Most binocular vision measures and tear-film signs did not change, apart from improved accommodative facility. The authors concluded that the rule was effective for reducing symptoms and that two weeks was too short to change binocular vision or dry eye signs.[4]
The study was small, with 29 participants and a two-week intervention. Other human research consists of prevalence surveys and reviews of management.[3][5][13]

Eye area aesthetics, including under-eye darkness, redness and a fatigued look, are a frequent topic in appearance communities, and screen time is a commonly mentioned contributor to tired-looking eyes. The 20-20-20 rule appears in these discussions as a zero-cost habit alongside sleep, hydration and lubricating drops. Reminder apps that time the breaks have been developed for desktop and phone, and a 2025 Hacker News post presented one that syncs break timing across devices.[8]

Other measures described for screen comfort include deliberate blinking, artificial tears for dry eye, adjusting screen brightness to the room and reducing glare, and correcting refractive error with prescription or computer glasses set for screen distance [6][5][3]. Wikipedia notes that double-blind trials of blue-light-filtering lenses found no benefit for digital eye strain, and that regular breaks and the 20-20-20 rule are listed alongside such measures [1]. The AAO distinguishes computer glasses, which are prescription lenses set for screen distance, from blue-light-blocking glasses [6].

Reviews also treat digital eye strain and dry eye disease as related but distinct, with a 2026 narrative review reporting that reduced blinking appears driven largely by the cognitive demands of the task [11].

The habit involves no products or procedures, and reviews describe digital eye strain symptoms as typically transient, though they may be frequent and persistent.[3] Persistent or worsening eye symptoms are generally a reason for an eye examination, since uncorrected refractive error and binocular vision problems are among the causes of digital eye strain.[3][6]

lore.intro: In appearance communities the rule is mentioned as one of the simple habits for reducing eye fatigue and keeping the eyes looking rested; the claims are mostly about comfort and eye-area appearance.

claims.claim: Look-away breaks make eyes look less tired and red
The 20-20-20 rule reduces digital eye strain symptoms
Blinking deliberately during breaks keeps eyes lubricated

timeline.event: Optometrist Jeffrey Anshel says he devised the 20-20-20 rule around this time while lecturing on computer vision stress [7].
Anshel's book Visual Ergonomics in the Workplace is first published [7].
A review in Optometry Times says no peer-reviewed study had evaluated the rule, and a review describes digital eye strain prevalence as possibly 50 percent or more among computer users [7][3].
COVID-19 lockdowns bring surveys of digital eye strain among students attending online classes [14][13].
A 29-person study of reminder software based on the rule reports symptom improvements during use [4]; a TFOS Lifestyle report reviews the digital environment and the ocular surface [9].
A Show HN post presents an app that syncs screen breaks between devices [8].
A systematic review and meta-analysis estimates global digital eye strain prevalence at 63 percent [10].
